get.summary: Get a list of all vision states.
Get the delivery measures over a window, computed from deployment records.
get.description:
Returns **deployment frequency** and **change failure rate**, plus an `unavailable` list naming the measures this module cannot compute yet and why — read that list rather than treating a missing measure as zero.

Two caveats worth carrying into any answer. **Production-scoped measures depend on environment categories**, not names, so a deployment into an environment whose category is not Production does not count toward deployment frequency. And **change failure rate is a proxy**: a pipeline run that failed before reaching production is a failure that was *prevented*, while a real change failure is a deployment that succeeded and then broke something — which the pipeline has no way to know. Report it as approximate rather than as the metric.

get.summary: Get version activity over a window — what was **cut and shipped**, measured from versions rather than deployments.
get.description:
Separate from `DeliveryMetrics_GetDeliveryMetrics`, which measures deployments: a product that ships continuously has a healthy cadence here whether or not its pipeline is recorded in Wayd.

Scoping to a product covers **that node and everything beneath it**, so a product line rolls up its children. Omit `productId` for the whole catalog.

Returns:
- `scope` — the selected product (null for the whole catalog) and `releasableNodeCount`, the denominator for judging the rest: three releases a week means something different across four products than across forty.
- `frequency` — `count`, `windowDays`, `perWeek`, and `previousPerWeek` for the equal window just before. **A null previous value means nothing shipped then** — the change is unknowable, so do not report it as a rise from zero.
- `cutToReleased` — `averageDays`, the elapsed time from cut to release in (fractional) days, with `measuredCount` of `releasedCount` and `previousAverageDays`. Versions released without ever being cut (imports and backfills do this) carry no latency and are excluded rather than counted as zero, so say how much of the window the average speaks for.
- `activity` — the subtree depth-first, one row per node with `depth` and `isReleasable`. Groupings appear so the hierarchy reads but never release anything themselves. Every releasable node in scope is listed even if it shipped nothing — that is part of the answer. `days` lists only days with a release: `released`, and `withdrawn` (how many of that day's versions have since been withdrawn — a count, not a rate).

parameters.name: from
parameters.description:
Any instant on the window's first day, read as a day in timeZone. An instant
rather than a date because the generated client types every date parameter as a JavaScript
`Date` and sends `toISOString()`, which no `LocalDate` binder accepts. The caller
sends the start of its local day, which lands on that day in its own zone.

parameters.name: to
parameters.description: Any instant on the window's last day, which is inclusive.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description: The ID of the product to scope the delivery overview to. Omit for the whole catalog.

parameters.name: timeZone
parameters.description:
The IANA zone whose days the window and the daily buckets are, normally the viewer's. Defaults
to UTC.

get.summary: Get what has happened to versions and packages lately, most recent first — a feed answering "what shipped recently?".
get.description:
**One entry per record**, at its latest status change, not one per transition; the record's own status history has the rest.

Each entry has `kind` (Version or ReleasePackage), `recordId`/`recordKey`, `label` (the version number or the package's own version, free text), `product` (null for a package, which spans several), `statusName` as the organization named it, `alias` (its well-known meaning — 10 Ready, 11 Released, 12 Withdrawn — which is what to reason on, since names are per-organization), `changedOn` (an instant), `releasedAt` (an instant) where the record has shipped (so a withdrawal says what it pulled), and `componentCount` for a package.

Read from status transitions rather than the records' own dates, which carry no time of day. **Scoping to a product covers its subtree and leaves packages out entirely.**

get.summary: List the deployment environments defined for the organization.
get.description: Environments are defined once and any product can deploy into any of them. Each carries a **category** and a **ring order**, so progressive rollout is representable. Filter by category rather than matching on names, which are free text.

post.summary: Define a deployment environment.
post.description: The **category** is what every production-scoped measure counts on, so set it deliberately rather than relying on the name. **Ring order** places the environment in a progressive rollout sequence — lower rings are reached first.

get.summary: Get what is running in each environment right now, in rollout order (lowest ring first).
get.description:
Answers "what version of X is in production?" and "how far has this got?" in one call.

Each environment lists `running`: **one entry per product**, never per package. A package deployment is expanded into its manifest and each component takes its own product's slot, so two successive bundles carrying the same component do not both show as running. Each entry is the **latest deployment that succeeded and was not rolled back** — a failed attempt leaves its predecessor running, and a rollback takes its own deployment out and leaves the one before it in. So "what is here" and "what happened last" differ: check `hasFailedAttemptSince`, true when a later deployment touching that product failed or was rolled back there.

Each entry carries `versionLabel` (always set, free text), `version` (null for a packaged component never cut as a version in Wayd), `package` (set when it arrived inside one), `artifactId`, `deployedAt`, and the `deploymentId`/`deploymentKey` it was read from. An empty `running` list means nothing has ever succeeded into that environment — a complete answer, not missing data.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of deployment environments to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Each row is created active unless IsActive is false, in which case it is created and then retired — for the environments a historical backfill's deployments still point at.

put.summary: Update an environment's name, category or ring order.
put.description:
**This is a whole-record overwrite — send every field, including ones you are not changing.**

Changing the category is not an ordinary edit: each deployment **froze** the category of the environment it went into, so reclassifying changes where *future* deployments count and leaves past ones exactly as they were. A staging environment promoted to production does not retroactively inflate deployment frequency. Refused on a retired environment.

delete.summary: Permanently delete an environment **and every deployment into it**, with their status history.
delete.description: The delivery measures and rollout stop counting those deployments. For an environment defined by mistake, or when the user asks to purge history — otherwise retire it with `DeploymentEnvironments_SetActive`, which keeps them. The `deploymentCount` from `DeploymentEnvironments_GetDeploymentEnvironments` says how many would go; state it before confirming. Needs the environment Delete permission, and — when the environment has any deployments — the delivery Delete permission as well.

put.summary: Retire an environment or reinstate one.
put.description:
**Retire rather than delete** unless the user explicitly wants the history gone: deleting an environment takes every deployment into it with it, while retiring keeps them.

A retired environment is no longer offered as a deployment target, but it and every deployment recorded against it are kept, and those deployments keep counting toward the measures they already count toward. Editing and reclassifying are refused on a retired environment, so reinstate it first if you need to change it.

get.summary: List deployments, most recently started first.
get.description: Each carries either a version or a package, never both. Filtering by environment category is how to scope to production, because environment *names* are free text and endlessly varied (`prod`, `Production`, `prd`, `live`) while the category is fixed.

post.summary: Record a deployment beginning.
post.description:
**Supply exactly one of versionId or packageId — never both, never neither.** The request is refused otherwise. Where a package exists it is the unit that shipped, so deploy the package rather than each component version: one pipeline run counts once, not once per service.

Only an **active** environment is accepted. Leaving `startedAt` empty records the deployment as starting now, which is what a pipeline reporting in real time would do. The artifact identifier is the build that actually shipped — `4.8.2.008` where the version number is `4.8.2` — and two builds of one version are two deployments.

get.summary: Get one deployment in full — what it carried, the environment it reached, its frozen environment category, its artifact identifier and its outcome.
get.description: Accepts the deployment's UUID or its short key.

get.summary: Get a deployment's activity history, newest first: when it started and its outcome — succeeded, failed or rolled back.
get.description: Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

get.summary: Get a deployment's status change history, newest first.
get.description: Each entry reports the status names as they were at the time.

get.summary: Get the status workflow a deployment currently moves through.
get.description: The workflow's statuses, the moves it allows and the conditions on each, with the moves the deployment's actions make, as the workflow's own detail returns them. Readable by anyone who can view the deployment, so its status history can be drawn on the workflow without the settings permission.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of deployments to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Each row names its version or package by id and its environment by name, and is walked to the outcome it describes with the timestamps it carries: no outcome leaves it in flight, Succeeded and Failed complete it, and RolledBack records a success and then the rollback. A build number is never resolved to a version.

post.summary: Record that a deployment reached its environment.
post.description: Offered only while the deployment is still in flight — once it has succeeded or failed, neither can be recorded again; a success can still be rolled back with `Deployments_RollBack`. There is no edit on a deployment — it records something that happened. **In production this also marks what shipped as released**: an unreleased version, or a package and the versions that changed in it, becomes Released at the completion. A released moment already recorded is never replaced.

post.summary: Record that a deployment did not reach its environment.
post.description: Offered only while the deployment is still in flight — once it has succeeded or failed, neither can be recorded again; a success can still be rolled back with `Deployments_RollBack`. Note this is a deployment that *failed to arrive* — a deployment that succeeded and then broke something is a rollback, not a failure, and the distinction matters because change failure rate counts the second kind.

delete.summary: Permanently delete a deployment and its status history.
delete.description: Allowed in any state. **The delivery measures and rollout stop counting it**, so this is for a deployment recorded by mistake or for purging a retired product's history — a deployment that really failed or was rolled back must be recorded with `Deployments_Fail` or `Deployments_RollBack` instead. Needs the delivery Delete permission.

post.summary: Record that a deployment reached its environment and was then reverted.
post.description: Offered only for a deployment that succeeded: one still in flight, failed, or already rolled back is refused. Distinct from a failure: this one arrived and then had to be undone, which is the signal change failure rate is computed from.

get.summary: List products from the catalog, ordered by name.
get.description:
Returns a **flat list, not a tree** — each product carries its parent as a reference, so build the hierarchy client-side.

Two filter behaviours worth knowing. `parentId` matches **direct children only**, not a whole subtree, and there is no way to ask for root nodes: omitting it returns everything rather than only roots. `tagId` is repeatable and combines as **AND, not OR** — passing a Platform tag and a Compliance tag returns products carrying both.

Each product reports `isReleasable`, flattened from its type, which is what decides whether versions can be cut against it.

post.summary: Add a product to the catalog.
post.description:
The **type** decides what the node can do — most consequentially whether versions can be cut against it — and must be an active type. Omit the parent to create a root node.

The external identifier is the node's id in whatever system owns it: a repository, a pipeline, a registry package. Capturing it now makes reconciling against a later automated feed a matching problem rather than a re-authoring one.

get.summary: Get one product in full — its type, parent, status, tags, external identifier, and whether its type allows versions to be cut against it.
get.description: Accepts the product's UUID or its short key.

get.summary: Get a product's activity history, newest first: every change recorded on the product — details, type, parent, status, tags and external link — plus a child product moving in or out, listed as a related entry raised on that child.
get.description: Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

get.summary: Get a product's status change history, newest first.
get.description: Each entry reports the status names as they were at the time, so a status renamed since does not rewrite the past.

get.summary: Get the status workflow a product currently moves through.
get.description: The workflow's statuses, the moves it allows and the conditions on each, as the workflow's own detail returns them. Readable by anyone who can view the product, so its status history can be drawn on the workflow without the settings permission.

get.summary: Get the statuses a product can be moved to, in the order an administrator laid the lifecycle out rather than alphabetically.
get.description:
**Call this before Products_ChangeStatus**: that tool needs a status UUID, statuses are per-organization configuration with no fixed list, and any id outside this workflow is refused.

Pass `productId` to get only the moves that product's workflow allows from its current status — a workflow can restrict which status may move to which, and a move outside them is refused. Each move then lists its `conditions`: `RequiresReason` means Products_ChangeStatus must be given a `reason`. Without `productId`, every status in the workflow is returned, with no conditions.

parameters.name: productId
parameters.description:
A product whose allowed moves to return, excluding its current status. Omit for every status in
the workflow.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of products to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.

Submit a csv file of product dependencies to import. Applied product by product: a product's rows apply together or not at all. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.

put.summary: Update a product's name and description.
put.description:
**This is a whole-record overwrite of those two fields: an omitted description is cleared.**

Only the name and description. Type, parent, status, tags and the external link each have their own tool, because each carries a rule this one does not — and keeping the external link out means a rename cannot silently clear it.

delete.summary: Permanently delete a product.
delete.description:
**This is a hard delete, not a retirement.** Consider changing the status instead if the product merely stopped being current. It takes its status history with it; its activity history is kept.

Refused while anything depends on it, each with its own reason: it has **child products** (move or remove them first), it has **versions**, it appears in a **release package manifest**, or it is named on **either end of a product dependency**. The manifest check is separate from versions because a carried-forward manifest line often names a product with no version row at all. The dependency check counts **ended** dependencies too — deleting the product would erase the record of what relied on it.

Tag assignments are removed with the product. Status does not block deletion.

put.summary: Set or clear a product's identifier in the system that owns it — a repository, a pipeline, a registry package.
put.description:
Omitting the value unlinks; there is no separate unlink tool. Free text, max 256 characters, and **not required to be unique**: two products may carry the same identifier.

This is separate from the ordinary update because it answers a different question — not what the product is called, but which external record it corresponds to — and keeping it apart stops a rename from silently clearing it.

put.summary: Move a product to a different parent, or to the root by omitting the parent.
put.description:
**Refused if the new parent is the product itself or one of its own descendants** — that would make a cycle. Any type may parent any other; there are no allowed-parent rules.

**Also refused when the move would put two products with an open dependency between them above and below one another** — that relationship is composition, which the tree already records. End the dependency first (`Products_EndDependency`).

The move is listed in the activity history of the product and of both its old and new parent.

put.summary: Change a product's type.
put.description:
**Refused if the product has versions and the new type is not releasable** — the versions already cut against it would be left hanging off a node that cannot carry them. The target type must be active, unless it is the type the product already has.

Note this is gated on *versions*, not releases: releasability asks whether an artifact can be cut against a node, and a release is an announcement that may sit under any node.

put.summary: Move a product to a different status.
put.description:
**Call Products_GetStatusOptions first** — this needs a status UUID, and statuses are per-organization configuration rather than a fixed set. A status belonging to a different workflow is refused.

The workflow may restrict which status can move to which; a move it does not allow is refused with both statuses named. Pass the product's id to Products_GetStatusOptions to get only its allowed moves and what each needs. A move whose conditions include `RequiresReason` is refused without a `reason`, naming what is missing; ask the user for the reason rather than inventing one. The reason is recorded on the status history. The status name is frozen onto the history at the moment of the change, so renaming a status later does not rewrite what past entries read as.

post.summary: Apply a tag to a product.
post.description:
Tags live in categories — axes such as Platform or Compliance — and a category decides whether a product may carry more than one of its tags.

**On a single-value axis this silently replaces the existing tag rather than refusing.** The call succeeds, and the tag the product previously carried on that axis is gone. Read the product first if that matters. On a multi-value axis the tag joins the others.

Both the tag and its category must be active. Applying a tag the product already carries succeeds and changes nothing.

delete.summary: Remove a tag from a product.
delete.description: Succeeds whether or not the product carried it, and an inactive tag can still be removed.

get.summary: Get what a product depends on (`dependsOn`) and what depends on it (`usedBy`).
get.description:
Accepts the product's UUID or its short key.

**Rolled up across everything beneath the product.** A link from one of its children to an outside product appears under `dependsOn`, and a link with both ends inside the product's own subtree appears in **neither** list — from outside, that is the product depending on itself. So reading a product line answers "what does this line rely on from elsewhere", and reading a leaf service answers it for that service alone.

Each entry carries both ends whichever list it is in — `product` (the one with the dependency) and `dependsOnProduct` — so a rolled-up row says which descendant it starts or lands on. `productPath` and `dependsOnProductPath` give each end's full ancestry, root first, down to its parent. Also `strength` (1 Hard: stops working without it; 2 Soft: degrades but keeps working), `description`, `startsOn`, and `endsOn` (null while it still holds).

`interactionStyles` lists how the product reaches the one it depends on — `Synchronous`, `Asynchronous`, or both. It refines `strength`: a Hard **synchronous** dependency caps the consumer's availability at the provider's, while a Hard **asynchronous** one turns the provider's downtime into a backlog the consumer works through afterwards. **`null` means nobody has recorded them, not that there are none** — do not read it as evidence either way.

Ended dependencies are left out unless `includeEnded` is true. An empty answer means no dependency has been recorded, not that none exists — they are entered by hand or by import.

post.summary: Record that a product depends on another.
post.description:
Returns the new dependency's id.

Record the **most specific product known** — the service that makes the call, not the platform it belongs to — since the read side rolls links up to every ancestor anyway. A product cannot depend on itself, nor on anything above or below it in the tree: that is composition, which the tree already records.

**Strength has no default and must be chosen deliberately**: Hard if the product stops working without it, Soft if it degrades or loses a feature but keeps working. Attributing a provider's downtime to its consumers reads this, so guessing either way misstates impact — ask if the person has not said.

`interactionStyles` says how the product reaches it — `Synchronous`, `Asynchronous`, or both, since a pair commonly calls for what it needs now and subscribes for what it needs eventually. Unlike strength it has no requirement to be set, but leaving it out records nothing rather than recording that there are none, so supply it when the person has said.

A product holds at most one open dependency on another product, and a later one on the same pair cannot overlap an earlier one. `startsOn` defaults to today, may be backdated, and cannot be in the future.

put.summary: Reword what a product's dependency is for, and record its interaction styles where none have been recorded.
put.description:
Terms and dates each have their own tool. Allowed on an ended dependency, since both describe the dependency rather than asserting anything about when it held.

**An omitted description is cleared, but omitted `interactionStyles` are left alone.** The asymmetry is deliberate: a description is prose somebody may want emptied, whereas styles are read when downtime is attributed, and omitting the field would otherwise erase them.

**This tool only fills a blank.** Changing styles already recorded is refused — that is a change of terms, which has to be dated, so use `Products_ChangeDependencyTerms`.

post.summary: Record that a product stopped depending on another.
post.description:
**The dependency is kept** and still counts for the period it held — this is the right tool when a dependency was true and no longer is. Use `Products_RemoveDependency` only for one that was never true.

`endsOn` is the last day it held: defaults to today, may be the day it started, and cannot be in the future.

put.summary: Change the terms a product's dependency holds on — its strength, how the product reaches it, or both.
put.description:
**This ends the current dependency and records a new one** on the new terms, so the history keeps when each set of terms held — and the response is the id of the dependency **now open**, which replaces the one you passed. Unchanged when the terms already match.

**`strength` is required and is the whole record's strength, not a delta.** Passing only `interactionStyles` still needs the current strength repeated, or you will silently change it.

**Omitted `interactionStyles` carry the recorded ones onto the new dependency** rather than clearing them.

Recording styles on a dependency that had none is the exception: nothing about the dependency changed, somebody finally wrote down how it had always worked, so it fills them in place, returns the **same** id, and `changedOn` is ignored. Dating that would split the period on a day nothing happened.

`changedOn` is the first day the new terms hold; the current dependency ends the day before. Defaults to today, must be after the day the dependency started, and cannot be in the future.

post.summary: **Delete** a dependency that was recorded by mistake.
post.description: Requires a reason saying why it was never true. Not for a dependency that stopped — `Products_EndDependency` keeps the history of when it held, and this erases it.

get.summary: List the tag categories and the tags in each.
get.description:
**Call this before Products_Tag**, which needs a tag UUID.

A category is an axis — Platform, Tech Stack, Compliance — and its `allowsMany` flag decides how tagging behaves. On an axis where `allowsMany` is false, applying a second tag **silently replaces** the first rather than refusing, so check this before tagging if the existing value matters.

Only active tags in active categories can be applied.

post.summary: Create a tag category — an axis such as Platform, Tech Stack or Compliance.
post.description: **`allowsMany` cannot be changed afterwards**, so choose it deliberately: it decides whether a product may carry several tags on this axis, or whether applying a second one silently replaces the first. Names must be unique. The category is created empty; add tags with ProductTagCategories_AddTag.

put.summary: Rename a tag category or change its description.
put.description: **An omitted description is cleared.** `allowsMany` is not here and cannot be changed after creation. Refused on a seeded system category. Names must stay unique.

delete.summary: Delete a tag category and its tags.
delete.description: Seeded system records cannot be modified or deleted, and a record in use cannot be deleted — deactivate it instead, which stops new use without breaking what already refers to it. A category counts as in use when any product is tagged along it, so this only removes an axis created by mistake and never applied.

put.summary: Take a tag category out of use, or put it back.
put.description:
Tags on an inactive category cannot be applied to a product, though products already carrying them keep them and can still have them removed.

As with product types, this **is** allowed on a seeded system category, unlike editing.

put.summary: Put the tag categories in a given order.
put.description: **The list must name every category exactly once** — a partial list is refused, so read them all first and send the complete sequence. Ordering is presentation only.

post.summary: Add a tag to a category.
post.description: Tag names must be unique within their axis, though the same name may appear on different axes. Refused on a seeded system category.

put.summary: Rename a tag or change its description.
put.description:
**An omitted description is cleared.** The tag must belong to the category named in the path. Names must stay unique within the axis. Refused on a seeded system category.

Renaming does not rewrite history: a product carrying the tag simply reports the new name.

delete.summary: Permanently delete a tag.
delete.description: The tag must belong to the category named in the path. Refused on a seeded system category, and refused while any product carries the tag — deactivate it with `ProductTagCategories_SetTagActive` instead, which stops new use without stripping it from the products that have it. The `productCount` on each tag from `ProductTagCategories_GetProductTagCategories` says whether it is in use.

put.summary: Take a tag out of use, or put it back.
put.description:
An inactive tag cannot be applied to a product, though products already carrying it keep it and can still have it removed. The tag must belong to the category named in the path.

**Refused on a seeded system category, and here there is no fallback** — unlike a category or a product type, an individual system tag can be neither modified nor retired. Deactivate the whole axis with `ProductTagCategories_SetActive` if it should stop being used.

get.summary: List the product types an organization recognises, in the order an administrator arranged them.
get.description:
**Call this before Products_Create or Products_Retype**, which both need a type UUID.

The flag that matters is `isReleasable`: it decides whether versions can be cut against products of this type. A product line or a platform is typically not releasable; a service, application or library is. It also gates retyping — a product with versions cannot be moved to a type that is not releasable.

Inactive types cannot be assigned to a product, though a product already carrying one keeps it.

post.summary: Define a product type.
post.description: **`isReleasable` is the consequential field** — it decides whether versions can be cut against products of this type, and it is what a product line or platform sets to false. Names must be unique. `order` is presentation only and implies no hierarchy.

put.summary: Update a product type.
put.description:
**This is a whole-record overwrite, and `isReleasable` is required — so renaming a type means resending its current releasability, and sending the wrong value silently changes whether versions can be cut against every product of this type.** Read the type first.

Refused on a seeded system type. Names must stay unique.

delete.summary: Delete a product type.
delete.description: Seeded system records cannot be modified or deleted, and a record in use cannot be deleted — deactivate it instead, which stops new use without breaking what already refers to it. A type is "in use" when any product carries it, so in practice this only removes a type created by mistake and never assigned.

put.summary: Take a product type out of use, or put it back.
put.description:
A deactivated type cannot be assigned to a product, but products already using it keep resolving it — which is why this is deactivation rather than deletion.

Unlike editing, this **is** allowed on a seeded system type: an organization that does not ship libraries should be able to hide that type without the seeder recreating it.

get.summary: List release packages — coordinated shipments such as `WAYD-2026.09.1`.
get.description: Unreleased first, then the most recently released. Use `containingVersionId` to answer "what did this version ship in?": a version carries no pointer back to its package, so membership is read from the manifest side rather than duplicated.

post.summary: Assemble a package and its manifest together.
post.description: **A package ships at least one component**, so the manifest is authored here rather than added afterwards — an empty one is refused. The package is versioned in its own right, separately from anything inside it. A component may appear only once in a manifest, though the same component version may appear in several different packages.

get.summary: Get one package in full, including its complete manifest — every component version it shipped, and whether each changed or was carried forward.
get.description: Accepts the package's UUID or its short key.

get.summary: Get a release package's activity history, newest first: its assembly, manifest amendments and status.
get.description: Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

get.summary: Get a package's status change history, newest first.
get.description: Each entry reports the status names as they were at the time, so a status renamed since does not rewrite the past.

get.summary: Get the status workflow a package currently moves through.
get.description: The workflow's statuses, the moves it allows and the conditions on each, with the moves the package's actions make, as the workflow's own detail returns them. Readable by anyone who can view the package, so its status history can be drawn on the workflow without the settings permission.

get.summary: Get the lifecycle actions a package's workflow allows from the status it holds.
get.description: Lists `MarkReleased` and `Withdraw` where the governing status workflow allows the move each one makes. A restricted workflow can leave out a move a company forbids — withdrawing a released package, say — and the action is then refused. This answers for the workflow only: the package's own rules still decide whether the action succeeds.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of release packages to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Takes two files: one row per package, and one row per manifest line naming the ImportId of the package it belongs to. Both are required — a package cannot be assembled without a manifest.

put.summary: Replace a package's manifest as a whole.
put.description: **This is a whole-set replacement: a line left out is removed from the package.** Components carry no identifier of their own and cannot be addressed individually, so read the package first and send back every line it should end up with. To add or change a few lines, use ReleasePackages_PatchManifest instead. The manifest closes once the package is released or withdrawn — what was in the box cannot be rewritten after the box shipped.

patch.summary: Add, change or drop lines in a package's manifest with a JSON Patch (RFC 6902), keeping every line it does not name.
patch.description: Prefer this to ReleasePackages_SetManifest for adding a component or changing one. The path is /components, a list of lines each with productId, versionId (optional), version and kind (Changed or CarriedForward). `add` with `/components/-` appends one line; `replace` with `/components/<index>/version` changes one field of the line at that index in the order ReleasePackages_GetReleasePackage returns. To drop a line, `replace` /components with every line that should remain. A package keeps at least one line, and the manifest closes once the package is released or withdrawn. Confirm with the user before calling.

post.summary: Record that a package shipped, and close its manifest.
post.description: **A package with an empty manifest cannot be released.** This is not announcing anything to customers — that is Releases_MarkReleased on a release that carries this package.

put.summary: Fix a package's target date or released moment that was recorded wrongly.
put.description: The status does not move and the status history is left untouched — that is the point of having this separate from ReleasePackages_MarkReleased, which asserts the package shipped and refuses to run twice. **Both values are sent, so an omitted target date is cleared.** The released moment can be changed on a released package but **cannot be cleared**, and **cannot be added to a package that has not been released** — use ReleasePackages_MarkReleased for that. The target date is a calendar date; the released moment is an instant, so send the CI/CD timestamp with its offset as-is — no conversion to a local date. Refused on a withdrawn package.

delete.summary: Permanently delete a package with its manifest, its status history and **every deployment of it**.
delete.description: **Refused while any release lists it** — remove it with `Releases_SetContents` first; a released or withdrawn release's contents cannot change, so that release has to be deleted instead with `Releases_Delete`. The versions it names are separate records and are kept. The delivery measures and rollout stop counting those deployments. For a package assembled by mistake or when the user asks to purge history; otherwise withdraw it. Needs the delivery Delete permission.

post.summary: Pull a package.
post.description: Terminal, and it closes the manifest. A released package can still be withdrawn; a withdrawn one cannot be released. Withdrawing keeps the package and every deployment of it — prefer it to `ReleasePackages_Delete`.

get.summary: List product releases — the announcements made to customers, such as `Wayd 2026.09`.
get.description: A release is what was announced to customers, not what was built — for one artifact and its version number, use the Versions_* tools instead. Unannounced releases come first, then the most recently announced. Never ordered by the version label, which is free text and never parsed. Filtering by product deliberately excludes releases that name no product: one spanning product lines belongs to no single product, so listing it under one would misstate what that product announced.

post.summary: Draft a release — the announcement, before it carries anything.
post.description: A release is what was announced to customers, not what was built — for one artifact and its version number, use the Versions_* tools instead. Contents are attached afterwards with Releases_SetContents, because an announcement is commonly drafted before anyone knows which versions will make it. The product is optional and usually names a product *line* rather than a leaf; leave it empty for a release spanning product lines. Unlike a version, a release is not restricted to releasable product types.

get.summary: Get one release in full, including everything it announces: the packages it shipped and the versions it carries directly.
get.description: Each contents entry reports its own shipped date, which is what tells you whether the release can be announced yet. A release is what was announced to customers, not what was built — for one artifact and its version number, use the Versions_* tools instead. Accepts the release's UUID or its short key.

get.summary: Get a release's activity history, newest first: every change recorded on the release — details, contents, dates and status.
get.description: Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

get.summary: Get a release's status change history, newest first.
get.description: Each entry reports the status names as they were at the time, so a status renamed since does not rewrite the past. Correcting a date leaves this untouched — that is the point of having a separate action for it.

get.summary: Get the status workflow a release currently moves through.
get.description: The workflow's statuses, the moves it allows and the conditions on each, with the moves the release's actions make, as the workflow's own detail returns them. Readable by anyone who can view the release, so its status history can be drawn on the workflow without the settings permission.

get.summary: Get the lifecycle actions a release's workflow allows from the status it holds.
get.description: Lists `MarkReleased`, `RevertRelease` and `Withdraw` where the governing status workflow allows the move each one makes. A restricted workflow can leave out a move a company forbids — reverting a release, say — and the action is then refused. This answers for the workflow only: the release's own rules (it cannot be announced while it carries something unshipped) still decide whether the action succeeds.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of releases to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Takes two files: one row per release, and one row per thing it announces, naming the ImportId of the release it belongs to. The contents file is optional — an empty release is a legitimate state. A release marked released is refused while anything it carries has not shipped.

put.summary: Update a release's descriptive fields.
put.description: **This is a whole-record overwrite: an omitted field is cleared.** Send every value the release should end up with, including ones you are not changing — omitting the product makes the release span product lines, and omitting the notes deletes them. The dates and the contents are not here; each has its own tool because each carries a rule this one does not.

delete.summary: Permanently delete a release in any state, with its list of contents and its status history.
delete.description: **The versions and packages it listed are kept** — only the release and its links to them go. For a release created by mistake, or when the user asks to purge history; a real announcement that was retracted is `Releases_Withdraw`. Deleting an announced release is also how a package it lists becomes deletable, since its contents cannot otherwise change. Needs the release Delete permission.

put.summary: Set everything a release announces — the packages it shipped and the versions it carries directly — in one call.
put.description:
**This is a whole-set replacement of both routes: anything left out is removed, and sending two empty lists clears the release entirely.** Read the release first and send back the full intended result, not just what you are adding. To add or remove a few entries, use Releases_PatchContents instead.

Contents arrive two ways and a release may use both: packages (the usual route, since a package is the deployment unit) and versions carried directly (for a single artifact that shipped alone, where nobody assembled a package).

**A version shipping inside one of the supplied packages cannot also be carried directly** — that would announce the same shipment twice. The rule is judged against what the release ends up containing, so moving a version out of the direct list and into a package that ships it is allowed in this one call. A manifest line naming no version record covers nothing and never conflicts.

An empty release is legitimate rather than a draft: a repackaging or a pricing change is announced with nothing deployed. Contents freeze once the release is announced or withdrawn.

patch.summary: Add or remove packages and directly carried versions on a release with a JSON Patch (RFC 6902), leaving the rest of its contents as they are.
patch.description: Prefer this to Releases_SetContents for any partial change. Paths are /packageIds and /versionIds. `add` with `/packageIds/-` appends one package id; to remove, `replace` the whole list with the set that should remain — never remove by index. A list the patch does not name keeps its contents. The release's rules apply to the result exactly as Releases_SetContents applies them: a version shipping inside one of its packages cannot also be carried directly, and contents freeze once the release is announced or withdrawn. Confirm with the user before calling.

put.summary: Move or clear a release's target date.
put.description: Omitting the date records that the release is no longer targeted, which is a different statement from never having set one. Refused on a release in a terminal status.

put.summary: Fix a release's target or announced date that was recorded wrongly.
put.description: The status does not move and the status history is left untouched — that is the point of having this separate from Releases_MarkReleased, which asserts the release moved and refuses to run twice. **Both dates are sent, so an omitted target date is cleared.** The announced date cannot be cleared once set: an announced release with no announced date contradicts its own status — revert it instead. There is no cut date to correct; a release is never cut.

post.summary: Record that a release was announced to customers.
post.description: **Refused while the release carries a version or package that has not shipped** — telling customers a release is out while something inside it has not gone anywhere is the one claim a release can make that its own contents contradict. Call Releases_GetRelease first and check each contents entry's shipped date; release the outstanding ones, or remove them from this release. An empty release announces normally. Shipping and announcing are separate acts, so this date is commonly later than the date the contents shipped.

post.summary: Retract a release after it was announced.
post.description: Terminal, and it says **nothing about the versions it carried** — an artifact that shipped has shipped whatever the market was later told, so a version that was itself pulled is withdrawn on its own record. Use this only when a real announcement was retracted; if the release was marked announced by mistake and never actually went out, use Releases_Revert instead.

post.summary: Record that a release marked as announced was **not in fact announced** — the wrong record was updated, and it never went out.
post.description: Returns the release to a live status and clears its announced date. A reason is required, unlike a withdrawal's optional one: this contradicts something the append-only history already asserts, so the record has to say why. Do not use this for a release that really was announced and then retracted — that is Releases_Withdraw.

get.summary: List versions — the artifacts that were built, such as `Wayd API 4.12.0`.
get.description: A version is one artifact that was built, not the announcement made to customers — for that, use the Releases_* tools instead. Everything not yet shipped comes first, then what has shipped, newest first: what is still coming is usually what you are looking for. Never ordered by the version number, which is free text and never parsed — `4.8.2` and `2026.04` are both just labels. There is no package filter here: a version carries no pointer to the package it shipped in, so ask that question from the packages side with ReleasePackages_GetReleasePackages.

post.summary: Record a version against a product.
post.description: A version is one artifact that was built, not the announcement made to customers — for that, use the Releases_* tools instead. The product is required and **must be of a releasable type** — a version is a cut of something that ships, so the API refuses a product line or other non-releasable node. Only the target date is set here; cutting and releasing are their own actions, because each records something that happened and each carries its own rule.

get.summary: Get one version in full — its product, version number, and its target date and its cut and released moments.
get.description: A version is one artifact that was built, not the announcement made to customers — for that, use the Releases_* tools instead. Accepts the version's UUID or its short key.

get.summary: Get a version's activity history, newest first: every change recorded on the version — details, dates and status.
get.description: Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

get.summary: Get a version's status change history, newest first — when it was cut, how long it sat ready before shipping, who moved it.
get.description: Each entry reports the status names as they were at the time, so a status renamed since does not rewrite the past. Correcting a date leaves this untouched.

get.summary: Get the status workflow a version currently moves through.
get.description: The workflow's statuses, the moves it allows and the conditions on each, with the moves the version's actions make, as the workflow's own detail returns them. Readable by anyone who can view the version, so its status history can be drawn on the workflow without the settings permission.

get.summary: Get the lifecycle actions a version's workflow allows from the status it holds.
get.description: Lists `Cut`, `MarkReleased`, `RevertRelease` and `Withdraw` where the governing status workflow allows the move each one makes. A restricted workflow can leave out a move a company forbids — withdrawing a released version, say — and the action is then refused. This answers for the workflow only: the version's own rules (a version cuts once; a withdrawn one cannot ship) still decide whether the action succeeds.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of versions to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Each row is planned against its product by id and walked to the state its moments describe: neither leaves it planned, a cut moment makes it ready, a released moment makes it released. Moments are ISO-8601 timestamps with an offset.

put.summary: Update a version's descriptive fields.
put.description: **This is a whole-record overwrite: an omitted field is cleared.** Send every value the version should end up with, including ones you are not changing. The dates are not here — each carries a rule the aggregate enforces, and folding them into a blanket save would hide which rule refused.

delete.summary: Permanently delete a version with its status history and **every deployment of it**.
delete.description: The delivery measures and rollout stop counting those deployments. **Refused while a release lists it or a package manifest names it** — remove it with `Releases_SetContents` or `ReleasePackages_SetManifest` first, or delete that release or package (an announced release or released package cannot change, so deleting it is the only way). For a version recorded by mistake or when the user asks to purge history; a real version that was pulled is `Versions_Withdraw`. Needs the delivery Delete permission.

put.summary: Move or clear a version's target date.
put.description: Omitting the date records that the version is no longer targeted, which is a different statement from never having set one. Refused on a released or withdrawn version.

put.summary: Fix a version's target date or cut or released moment that was recorded wrongly.
put.description: The status does not move and the status history is left untouched — that is the point of having this separate from Versions_Cut and Versions_MarkReleased, which assert the version moved and refuse to run twice. **All three are sent, so an omitted target date or cut moment is cleared.** The released moment cannot be cleared once set: a released record with no released moment contradicts its own status — revert it instead. A version cannot be released before it was cut. The target date is a calendar date; the cut and released moments are instants, sent with their offset exactly as the CI/CD system reports them. Refused on a withdrawn version.

post.summary: Record that a version was cut — scope is frozen and it is ready to ship.
post.description: **One-way: a version cannot be cut twice**, and a released or withdrawn version refuses it. Cutting is not a prerequisite for releasing: a version imported after the fact can be marked released without ever having been cut, which is why this is a separate action rather than a step.

post.summary: Record that a version shipped.
post.description: **This is not announcing it to customers** — that is Releases_MarkReleased on a release. A version can be marked released without ever having been cut, which is what makes importing historical versions possible; where it was cut, it cannot be released before it was cut. Refused on a withdrawn version.

post.summary: Pull a version.
post.description: Terminal. **A released version can still be withdrawn** — pulling something after it shipped is exactly the case this exists for — but a withdrawn one cannot be released. Use this only when a real version was pulled; if it was marked released by mistake and never actually shipped, use Versions_Revert instead.

post.summary: Record that a version marked as shipped did **not in fact ship** — the wrong record was updated.
post.description: Returns it to Ready, or to the initial status where it was never cut, and clears the released moment. A reason is required, unlike a withdrawal's optional one: this contradicts something the append-only history already asserts. Do not use this for a version that really shipped and was then pulled — that is Versions_Withdraw.

get.summary: Get a list of expenditure categories — how project spending is classified (for example Opex or Capex) — in every state.
get.description: Each carries its state (Proposed, Active, Archived), whether it is capitalizable and requires depreciation, and its accounting code. To pick a category for a project, ExpenditureCategories_GetOptions is lighter.

post.summary: Create an expenditure category.
post.description: It starts in Proposed state; a project can be given only an Active category, so activate it with ExpenditureCategories_Activate before use. Returns the new category's numeric id. Confirm with the user before calling.

get.summary: Get expenditure category details.
get.description: Takes the category's numeric id.

put.summary: Update an expenditure category's name, description, capitalizable and depreciation settings, and accounting code.
put.description: This is a whole-record update, not a patch: every field is overwritten from the request body, so an omitted accounting code is cleared and an omitted flag becomes false. Read the category first and echo back every value that should stay the same. Once the category is Active, `isCapitalizable` and `requiresDepreciation` are fixed and must be sent unchanged; an Archived category cannot be updated. The id in the body must match the id path parameter. Projects already using it see the change, so confirm with the user before calling.

delete.summary: Delete an expenditure category.
delete.description: Permanent, and only for a category still in Proposed state and not used by any project. An active category cannot be deleted; archive it instead (ExpenditureCategories_Archive). Confirm with the user before calling.

post.summary: Activate a proposed expenditure category so projects can use it.
post.description: **Activation fixes its capitalizable and depreciation settings**; the name, description and accounting code stay editable. Only a Proposed category can be activated, and an active one cannot be deleted. Confirm with the user before calling.

post.summary: Archive an active expenditure category, retiring it from new projects.
post.description: Projects already using it keep it. An archived category cannot be updated or reactivated. Only an Active category can be archived. Confirm with the user before calling.

get.summary: Get a lightweight list of expenditure category options for lookups.
get.description: Use this to resolve the expenditureCategoryId required when creating or updating a project.

get.summary: Get a list of project portfolios.

post.summary: Create a portfolio.
post.description: It starts in Proposed status — use Portfolios_Activate to make it active, which also stamps its start date. Role lists REPLACE the existing assignments for that role — they do not add to them. An omitted or empty list REMOVES everyone currently holding that role. Always read the current record first and pass back the full membership you intend to keep, including people you are not changing. Changes a record other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling.

get.summary: Get project portfolio details.
Get a portfolio's activity history, newest first: every change recorded on the portfolio itself — details, roles, scoring model, status.
get.description: Its programs and projects keep their own histories. Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of portfolios to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
Submit a csv file of PPM finalizations to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Completes or cancels programs and closes or archives portfolios, after their contents have been imported.

put.summary: Update a portfolio's name, description, and role assignments.
put.description: This is a whole-record update, not a patch: every field is overwritten from the request body, so omitting a field clears it. For a partial change, use Portfolios_Patch instead. Read the record first and echo back every value that should stay the same. Role lists REPLACE the existing assignments for that role — they do not add to them. An omitted or empty list REMOVES everyone currently holding that role. Always read the current record first and pass back the full membership you intend to keep, including people you are not changing. The id in the body must match the id path parameter. Requires delivery leadership — the caller must be an Owner or Manager of the record or of an ancestor; a permission claim alone is not enough. Changes a record other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling.

Place them with anchors: `afterProjectId` is the project that will sit immediately above the batch, `beforeProjectId` the one immediately below. Give both to drop between two projects, only `beforeProjectId` (the current first project) to move to the top, or only `afterProjectId` (the current last project) to move to the bottom. At least one anchor is required, an anchor cannot be in the batch, and `afterProjectId` must rank above `beforeProjectId`. Projects already between the anchors keep their order after the batch. Ranks are opaque fractional values; never show them to the user. Requires delivery leadership — the caller must be an Owner or Manager of the portfolio; a permission claim alone is not enough. The ranking is shared, so confirm the new order with the user before calling. Takes the portfolio's UUID only, not a key.

Caller must be the project, parent portfolio, or parent program owner or manager. To recommend a check, first gather the evidence with Projects_GetHealthCheckEvidence: the plan summary, overdue tasks, stages past their end, the delivery forecast, the latest check and the activity since it. Take the worst status any signal supports: Unhealthy for a forecast chance below 50% or an 85% date well past the project's end, a Blocked by Dependency outcome, a large share of tasks overdue, or a stage past its end with substantial work left; AtRisk for a chance of 50–80% or an 85% date just past the end, several overdue tasks, a predecessor with a high shareOfTrialsSettingFinish, or stage progress lagging elapsed time; otherwise Healthy. delete.summary: Delete a project.

Only a project in Proposed status that has never moved out of Proposed can be deleted — one that was approved or activated and later reverted stays undeletable, so cancel it instead (Projects_Cancel). get.summary: Gather the evidence for recommending a project health check in one read: the project, plan summary, overdue tasks with keys, stages flagged when past their end, the delivery forecast, the latest check, and activity since it.
get.description: Use it first when recommending a health check. `overdueTasks` are the open tasks the plan summary counts as overdue. A stage with `pastEndNotComplete` ended before `asOf` and is neither completed nor canceled. `forecast` is the Projects_GetForecast result against the project's end, or null with `forecastUnavailableReason` when delivery forecasting is off — leave it out of the classification then. Critical-path evidence is never available (`criticalPathUnavailableReason`); never read that as "no critical tasks". `activitySinceLatestCheck` holds the project's own changes after the latest check, newest first, without tasks or stages; `activityTruncated` means there was more. The forecast options are those of Projects_GetForecast. Take the worst status any signal supports: Unhealthy for a forecast chance below 50% or an 85% date well past the project's end, a Blocked by Dependency outcome, a large share of tasks overdue, or a stage past its end with substantial work left; AtRisk for a chance of 50–80% or an 85% date just past the end, several overdue tasks, a predecessor with a high shareOfTrialsSettingFinish, or stage progress lagging elapsed time; otherwise Healthy. A forecast whose outcome is neither Forecast nor Blocked by Dependency and that has no dates is left out of the classification too.Draft a note (at most 1024 characters) citing this evidence and present the status, the signal that set it and the note. Logging is a separate Projects_CreateProjectHealthCheck call, made only after the user confirms and only where that tool is listed.

get.description: Returns an `outcome` (Forecast, Done, Not Enough History, Blocked by Dependency, Cannot Forecast, Nothing Remaining); on Forecast, completion `percentiles` (a `date` per `confidence`) and `chanceOfFinishingByTargetDate` (0 to 1) against `targetDate` when given, else the project's planned end. `excludedWorkItems` could not be forecast (see `issues`), which makes the dates a lower bound; `dependencies` gives each predecessor's `shareOfTrialsSettingFinish`. Requires the delivery-forecasting feature flag; returns 404 when it is off.

post.description: Only for a project with no lifecycle yet — when one is assigned, use Projects_ChangeLifecycle. `lifecycleId` must be an Active lifecycle (ProjectLifecycles_GetProjectLifecycles with state Active). Each lifecycle stage becomes a project stage, in order, ready to hold tasks; approving a project (Projects_Approve) requires a lifecycle. Rejected for a completed or canceled project. Requires delivery leadership — the caller must be an Owner or Manager of the record or of an ancestor; a permission claim alone is not enough. Confirm with the user before calling. Tasks in an unmapped stage go to the new lifecycle's first stage. Only for a project that already has a lifecycle — otherwise use Projects_AssignLifecycle. Rejected for a completed or canceled project. Requires delivery leadership — the caller must be an Owner or Manager of the record or of an ancestor; a permission claim alone is not enough. Show the user the mapping and the stage data that will be lost, and confirm before calling. Takes the project's UUID only, not a key.

put.description: This is a whole-record update, not a patch: every field is overwritten from the request body, so an omitted date is cleared and an omitted progress becomes 0. For a partial change, use Projects_PatchStage instead. Read the stage first (Projects_GetProjectStage) and echo back every value that should stay the same. `status` is a task status id from Tasks_GetTaskStatuses. `plannedStart` and `plannedEnd` are set together or both left null, and must cover the dated top-level tasks in the stage. `assigneeIds` REPLACES the stage's assignees — an omitted or empty list removes every assignee; only an explicit null leaves them unchanged. Assignee ids are employee ids. The stage's name comes from its lifecycle and cannot be changed here. Requires the project update permission. Confirm with the user before calling. Takes the project's and the stage's UUIDs, not keys.

patch.summary: Partially update a project stage using JSON Patch (RFC 6902).
patch.description: Paths are the update's camelCase fields: /description, /status (a task status id from Tasks_GetTaskStatuses), /plannedStart and /plannedEnd (set both, or clear both), /progress, /assigneeIds. `replace` changes a field; `add` with `/assigneeIds/-` appends one id; to remove from the list, `replace` it with the set that should remain — never remove by index. A field the patch does not name keeps its value. Assignee ids are employee ids. Confirm with the user before calling.

get.summary: Get the scoring context for a project: the scoring model assigned to its portfolio (criteria, scales, and outputs), whether that model has been archived, and the project's current score.
get.description: The scoring model is null when the project's portfolio has no model assigned, which means the project cannot be scored.

get.summary: Get the scoring history for a project — every score ever recorded, each with its headline value, the model used, who scored it, and when.
get.description: Returns headline values only; use Projects_GetScore for a single score's full per-criterion rating breakdown.

post.summary: Record a score for a project against its portfolio's scoring model, returning the new score's id.
post.description: Read Projects_GetScoringContext first: it gives the model's criteria and scales, and a null model means the portfolio has none and the project cannot be scored. Rate **every** criterion in the model — one entry in `ratings` per criterion, by `criterionId`. A criterion with a scale is rated by `ratingLevelId`, one of that scale's levels; any other criterion by a numeric `value`. Each call adds a new score to the project's history and makes it the current score; earlier scores are kept, so to correct a score record a new one. Requires delivery leadership — the caller must be an Owner or Manager of the record or of an ancestor; a permission claim alone is not enough. Confirm the ratings with the user before calling. Takes the project's UUID only, not a key.

get.summary: Get one recorded project score in full.
get.description: Returns the frozen snapshot as it was at scoring time — every criterion rating and computed output value, plus the model name and version used. Because the snapshot is frozen, an old score reflects the model as it was then, not the model as it is now.

get.summary: Get a list of project tasks.

post.summary: Create a project task.

get.summary: Get project task details.

put.summary: Update a project task.
put.description: For a partial change, use Tasks_PatchProjectTask instead.

patch.summary: Partially update a project task using JSON Patch (RFC 6902).
patch.description: Prefer this to Tasks_UpdateProjectTask for any partial change. Paths are the update's camelCase fields: /name, /description, /statusId and /priorityId (ids from Tasks_GetTaskStatuses and Tasks_GetTaskPriorities), /assigneeIds, /progress, /parentId (a parent task, or the stage for a top-level task), /plannedStart and /plannedEnd (set both, or clear both), /plannedDate, /estimatedEffortHours. `replace` changes a field; `add` with `/assigneeIds/-` appends one id to a list; to remove from a list, `replace` the whole list with the set that should remain — never remove by index. A field the patch does not name keeps its value. Assignee ids are employee ids. Confirm with the user before calling.

delete.summary: Delete a project task.

put.summary: Update a project task's placement within a parent.
put.description: Moves a task, with its subtasks, to another place in the plan or reorders it among its siblings; nothing else about the task changes. `parentId` is a stage id (the task becomes a top-level task in that stage) or another task's id (it becomes that task's child); a milestone cannot be a parent, and a task cannot move under itself or its own subtasks. `order` is the 1-based position among the new parent's children; omit it to place the task last. Moving to another stage moves its subtasks too. `taskId` in the body must match the id path parameter, which takes the task's UUID only; the project accepts a UUID or key. Confirm with the user before calling.

get.summary: Get the critical path for the project.
get.description: Returns an ordered list of task IDs on the critical path.

post.summary: Add a dependency to a task.
post.description: Creates a finish-to-start dependency where the specified task is the predecessor.

delete.summary: Remove a dependency from a task.
delete.description: Removes the finish-to-start dependency between the predecessor and successor tasks.

get.summary: Get a list of all task types.
Get a list of all task statuses.
Get a list of all task priorities.
Get a list of strategic initiatives.
get.description: Optionally filter by status and/or portfolioId.

post.summary: Create a strategic initiative.
post.description: It starts in Proposed status. `portfolioId` must be an active or on-hold portfolio (Portfolios_GetPortfolioOptions resolves a name). `start` and `end` are calendar dates, end on or after start. `sponsorIds` and `ownerIds` are employee ids. Add KPIs afterwards with StrategicInitiatives_CreateKpi and link projects with StrategicInitiatives_ManageProjects. Returns the new initiative's id and key. Confirm with the user before calling.

get.summary: Get strategic initiative details, including its portfolio, date range, sponsors, and owners.

Get a strategic initiative's activity history, newest first: every change recorded on the initiative — details, roles, timeline, status, linked projects, and its KPIs with their targets, checkpoint plans and measurements.
get.description: Each entry has a `category` (Created, Updated, ScheduleChanged, StatusChanged, StateChanged, Health, Removed, Baseline), an `actorKind` (User, System, Import, Sync, Anonymous) with the acting `employee` when there is one, a `timestamp`, a one-line `summary`, and a `payload`: the event's fields as a JSON string. A change carries both ends, the value before and after. People in a payload are employee ids, not user ids. A Baseline entry marks where tracking began for a record that already existed, holding what it looked like then; nothing before it was recorded. An entry with `isRelated: true` was raised on another record and is listed here because it concerns this one; `raisedOn` names that record, or is null where it could not be resolved (typically removed since). Paged: the response carries `totalCount` and `hasNextPage`.

post.summary: Submit a csv file of strategic initiatives to import. Returns the run — 200 once it has finished, 202 while it is still queued or running.
post.description: Optionally accepts a second csv of KPIs, whose rows name the ImportId of the initiative they belong to.

put.summary: Update a strategic initiative's name, description, dates, sponsors and owners.
put.description: This is a whole-record update, not a patch: every field is overwritten from the request body, so read the initiative first (StrategicInitiatives_GetStrategicInitiative) and echo back every value that should stay the same. Role lists REPLACE the existing assignments for that role — they do not add to them. An omitted or empty `sponsorIds` or `ownerIds` REMOVES everyone in that role; only an explicit null leaves it unchanged. Role ids are employee ids. The id in the body must match the id path parameter. Status, portfolio, KPIs and linked projects are not changed here. Checks permissions only, not delivery leadership. Changes a record other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling. Takes a UUID only, not a key.

delete.summary: Delete a strategic initiative.
delete.description: Permanent: its KPIs, checkpoints and measurements go with it, and its links to projects are removed (the projects themselves stay). Only a Proposed or Approved initiative can be deleted; an active or closed one cannot — cancel it instead (StrategicInitiatives_Cancel). Rejected when the portfolio is archived. Confirm with the user before calling. Takes a UUID only, not a key.

post.summary: Approve a proposed strategic initiative.
post.description: Changes a published status that other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling. Takes a UUID only, not a key.

post.summary: Activate an approved strategic initiative.
post.description: Changes a published status that other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling. Takes a UUID only, not a key.

post.summary: Complete an active or on-hold strategic initiative.
post.description: **Completing closes the initiative**, after which its KPIs and linked projects can no longer be added, edited, reordered, or removed. Changes a published status that other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling. Takes a UUID only, not a key.

post.summary: Cancel a strategic initiative.
post.description: **Cancelling closes the initiative**, after which its KPIs and linked projects can no longer be added, edited, reordered, or removed. Changes a published status that other people rely on, so confirm with the user before calling. Takes a UUID only, not a key.

get.summary: Get a list of all strategic initiative statuses.
get.description: Call this to resolve the integer enum values used by the status filter.

get.summary: Get the KPIs for a strategic initiative — the measures that define whether it succeeded.
get.description: Each KPI carries a starting (baseline) value, a target value, the latest actual value, and a computed progress percentage toward the target. targetDirection is Increase or Decrease; for a Decrease KPI a falling value is improvement, so never assume a lower number is worse.

post.summary: Create a KPI for a strategic initiative.
post.description: `strategicInitiativeId` in the body must match the id path parameter. `targetValue` is required and non-zero. `targetDirection` is Increase or Decrease, and a `startingValue`, when given, must be below the target for Increase and above it for Decrease. `prefix` and `suffix` (at most 8 characters each, such as `$` or `%`) are only for display. The KPI is added after the existing ones. Set its dated targets afterwards with StrategicInitiatives_ManageKpiCheckpointPlan. Rejected once the initiative is completed or canceled. Returns the new KPI's id and key. Confirm with the user before calling. Takes UUIDs only, not keys.

get.summary: Get a single KPI for a strategic initiative.

put.summary: Update a KPI's definition: name, description, starting and target values, display prefix and suffix, and target direction.
put.description: This is a whole-record update, not a patch: every field is overwritten from the request body, so an omitted description, starting value, prefix or suffix is cleared. Read the KPI first (StrategicInitiatives_GetKpi) and echo back every value that should stay the same. A `startingValue` must be below the target for Increase and above it for Decrease. Measurements and checkpoints are not changed here. `strategicInitiativeId` and `kpiId` in the body must match the path parameters. Rejected once the initiative is completed or canceled. Confirm with the user before calling. Takes UUIDs only, not keys.

delete.summary: Delete a KPI for a strategic initiative.
delete.description: Permanent: the KPI's checkpoints and every measurement recorded against it go with it. Rejected once the initiative is completed or canceled. Confirm with the user before calling. Takes UUIDs only, not keys.

post.summary: Reorder KPIs for a strategic initiative.
